debate.situation: You are the one who always proposes plans with a friend. Your time together is lovely, but when you stop texting, contact stops. What you know is the pattern; what you do not know is why: she may be a low-initiation person who values you, she may take your planning for granted, or something else may be going on. The decision is whether to say something, and it may depend less on whether to speak than on what you want from the friendship.

minds.title: The Over-functioner Spotter
minds.concern: Patterns in a relationship are kept alive by both people, so changing your own part, including speaking up calmly, is where your power lies.
minds.author: Harriet Lerner

minds.title: The Friendship Idealist
minds.concern: Real friendship is generous and unmetered, so counting texts risks turning a gift into an audit.
minds.author: Ralph Waldo Emerson

minds.title: The Fact-Story Separator
minds.concern: Pain comes from mixing what happened with the stories we attach to it; clarity means observing, naming needs, and making a specific request.
minds.author: Marshall Rosenberg

debate.speaker: The Over-functioner Spotter
debate.text: You are doing all the reaching, and that pattern holds only because you keep holding it up. Saying something is not an accusation; it is changing your own step in the dance. I would say it, calmly, and soon, before resentment leaks out sideways.
debate.author: Harriet Lerner
debate.basis: Basis: Harriet Lerner, The Dance of Connection

debate.speaker: The Friendship Idealist
debate.text: Soon is doing a lot of work there. She is lovely in person. Some people are bad at texting and wonderful at being present. Keeping score of who initiates may turn a gift into an audit. Why not keep giving and let the friendship breathe?
debate.author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
debate.basis: Basis: Ralph Waldo Emerson, Essays: First Series

debate.speaker: The Fact-Story Separator
debate.text: You are both skipping a step. The fact is that you plan and, when you stop, contact stops. Everything else, she does not care, she takes me for granted, is a story. Before anyone speaks or waits, sort which is which.
debate.author: Marshall Rosenberg

debate.speaker: The Over-functioner Spotter
debate.text: Fair, but a pattern is also a fact. If it has run for months, waiting is not neutral; it is a decision to keep carrying it. I would go further than Lerner here: a small experiment, like pausing your planning for a few weeks, may teach more than a speech.
debate.author: Harriet Lerner
debate.basis: Basis: Harriet Lerner, The Dance of Connection

debate.speaker: The Fact-Story Separator
debate.text: A silent test is a demand in disguise. You would be waiting for her to pass without telling her there is an exam. If the pause is just information, fine, but if you are secretly asking for proof, say the request out loud instead.
debate.author: Marshall Rosenberg

debate.speaker: The Fact-Story Separator
debate.text: Here is a reading, and you can reject it. When you write that nothing happens, the sting may be a worry that you matter less to her than she does to you. If so, you are after reassurance, not more texts, and no schedule would fix that.
debate.author: Marshall Rosenberg

debate.speaker: The Friendship Idealist
debate.text: A rival reading fits those same words. Perhaps a borrowed standard is steering you: the idea that real friends text back and forth all week. Yet you call the meetings lovely. If the standard is borrowed, the cure is to question the standard, not her.
debate.author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
debate.basis: Basis: Ralph Waldo Emerson, Essays: First Series

debate.speaker: The Over-functioner Spotter
debate.text: Notice the readings point to different actions. If it is a worry about mattering, say so, gently and about yourself. If it is a borrowed standard, you may have nothing to say. I concede speaking is not mandatory, but I still doubt the worry stays quiet forever.
debate.author: Harriet Lerner
debate.basis: Basis: Harriet Lerner, The Dance of Connection

debate.speaker: The Fact-Story Separator
debate.text: Then make it concrete. Something like: I notice I am usually the one proposing, and I would love it if you suggested something next time. That is an observation and a small request, with no verdict on her character and plenty of room for her to say no.
debate.author: Marshall Rosenberg

debate.speaker: The Friendship Idealist
debate.text: My worry is that a requested plan may feel like homework, when friends should give freely. But I grant this: if the request is small and she is truly free to decline, it respects her more than a silent audit would.
debate.author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
debate.basis: Basis: Ralph Waldo Emerson, Essays: First Series

debate.speaker: The Over-functioner Spotter
debate.text: So we narrow it. Say something once, lightly, about your own wish, and then watch what she does with it. We still disagree on whether that is a conversation or a trial, and on whether the pattern truly needs naming at all.
debate.author: Harriet Lerner
debate.basis: Basis: Harriet Lerner, The Dance of Connection

debate.clearer: The main insight is that there are two separate questions: what the pattern means, and what you want from this friendship. The minds disagreed over whether the sting is a worry about mattering or a borrowed standard of what friendship should look like, and that remains open; only you can recognize which, if either, fits. They also left open whether the right move is a light conversation or simply watching what happens. A possible self-reflection: if she initiated tomorrow, would the sting disappear, or would something remain?
debate.dependsOn: If the sting is mostly about wanting to know you matter, a short, kind, specific mention becomes more reasonable, because the pattern is not the real issue and silence will not answer it. If the lovely meetings leave you content and the text count only bothers you in the abstract, letting it go, or initiating without keeping score, becomes more reasonable, because nothing concrete is missing. If you are unsure how she would react, a low-stakes way to learn is to name one small preference once and see whether she responds warmly, awkwardly, or not at all. If the pattern has gone on a long time and resentment is building, waiting becomes the costlier option.
